pages.text: Contact Us - Data.gov Skip to main content An official website of the United States government Here's how you know Here's how you know The .gov means it's official. Federal government websites often end in .gov or .mil. Before sharing sensitive information, make sure you're on a federal government site. The site is secure. The https:// ensures that you are connecting to the official website and that any information you provide is encrypted and transmitted securely. Try the next-generation Data Catalog at catalog.data.gov and help shape it with your feedback. Data.gov is a metadata catalog. We provide information about federal datasets and links to where data is published. We do not own or manage the underlying data. If you have a question about a specific dataset, the publishing agency is the right contact. See the links below for answers to common questions before reaching out. Find and search for data # Search the full catalog at catalog.data.gov . Use the filters on the right side of the catalog to narrow results by geography, keyword, organization, publisher, or geospatial vs. non-geospatial data. Note: "Organizations" includes federal agencies as well as non-federal entities such as states and cities. Click any keyword tag on a dataset page to search for similar datasets. Many dataset pages include a link to the publishing agency's own landing page, which may provide additional context about the data. Data.gov links to data hosted by federal agencies. pages.text: Contexte - Journée des toilettes | Nations Unies Skip to main content UNICEF/Karel Prinsloo Qu’est-ce que la Journée mondiale des toilettes? La Journée mondiale des toilettes est organisée chaque année le 19 novembre afin d'encourager les actions en faveur de la réalisation de l’objectif de développement durable 6 (ODD 6): un accès universel à l’eau et à l’assainissement. Coordonnée par ONU-Eau, la Journée mondiale des toilettes est soutenue par des millions de personnes et d'institutions à travers le monde, qui diffusent des messages, organisent des événements et lancent des campagnes de sensibilisation. Pourquoi les toilettes sont-elles importantes ? L'accès à des services d’assainissement est un droit humain. Pourtant, des milliards d'êtres humains sont laissés pour compte, sans accès à des toilettes salubres, et en paient le prix fort, car cette situation a de lourdes conséquences pour leur santé, leur éducation, leurs moyens de subsistance et leur environnement. La crise planétaire de l'assainissement touche tout le monde, mais pas avec la même intensité. Ce sont les femmes, les filles et d'autres groupes vulnérables qui paient le plus lourd tribut. Que fait l'ONU pour contribuer à garantir l'accès universel à des toilettes sûres ? Describe the issue below: Description: License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2611.00150v1 [astro-ph.IM] 30 Oct 2026 [orcid=0009-0009-4239-7070] [orcid=0000-0002-8178-8463] [orcid=0000-0002-2720-7218] Contrastive Astromer: Two-Stage Contrastive Representation Learning for Astronomical Light Curve Classification Justin Minggan Wei mwei@fas.harvard.edu Pavlos Protopapas Guillermo Cabrera-Vives organization=School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Harvard University, city=Cambridge, state=MA, postcode=02138, country=USA organization=Department of Computer Science, Universidad de Concepción, addressline=Edmundo Larenas 219, city=Concepción, country=Chile Abstract Large astronomical surveys collect abundant light curves, but reliable class labels remain scarce. ASTROMER 2 learns from unlabeled light curves by reconstructing masked observations, yet this objective does not explicitly encourage class separation in a compact representation of each light curve. We introduce Contrastive Astromer, a two-stage approach that makes these representations more useful for classification without changing the ASTROMER 2 encoder architecture. First, unsupervised contrastive learning on single-band MACHO light curves brings together representations of augmented views of the same object. Supervised contrastive learning, supported by an auxiliary classification loss, then uses a separate labeled Alcock sample to strengthen class discrimination.

The differences of these scales from ITS-90 is typically small, but not necessarily negligible for reference-quality work. We describe conversion to ITS-90 from 34 different scales. These include not only the relatively well-known International Temperature Scales from 1968, 1948, and 1927, but also scales that have been used for cryogenic work at temperatures below the ranges of the older international scales, including the many scales that were based on the vapor pressure of helium. Many countries were surprised to see a first draft of a potential “cover decision” from the fortnight-long talks early on Monday afternoon, with more than four days of negotiation still to go. The text includes several proposals regarded as highly contentious by some countries, including a call to “immediately transition away from fossil fuels”. Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister, said: “It’s a genuine attempt to draw out parties on what they can support and what they can’t. pages.text: COP31: Pakistan's solar revolution has been so successful the national grid is crumbling Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Pakistan's solar revolution has been so successful the national grid is crumbling 5 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Carrie Davies Pakistan correspondent BBC Faizal Shahzad wants to buy several more solar panels to make his home in rural Punjab fully self-sufficient Jewellery, glimmering silverware, sofas and an air-conditioning unit. Three months after his wedding, Faisal Shahzad's home in rural Punjab is bursting with gifts from his bride's family, as part of the dowry. But the most prized possession is tucked under the bed: a 340W solar panel. "In the summer we ran it from 08:00 in the morning until the evening," he says, adding they didn't need to use grid power at all during the day. "We ran our air cooler on it all day." Pakistan has seen a boom in imported solar panels, which glisten from the rooftops of homes and hospitals; from farmers' fields to industrial complexes. From 2018 to 2025, the share of electricity generated from solar energy in the country rose from 1% to 28%, according to Pakistan-based think tank Renewables First, with some seven million households now owning panels. People used to gift motorbikes or other household items at weddings, Shahzad says. "Now they give a solar panel and an air cooler. It has almost become a must." Delegates from more than 190 countries are gathering in Turkey for climate talks, but the US will be absent Fiona Harvey Environment editor Sun 8 Nov 2026 11.00 GMT Last modified on Wed 11 Nov 2026 11.44 GMT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google As the planet faces unprecedented human-caused global heating, heads of government are meeting for the next fortnight for the latest round of climate talks. We ask why it matters and what is likely to be achieved. What is Cop31? From 9-20 November, world leaders, ministers and high-ranking officials from more than 190 countries are expected to convene in Antalya in Turkey, for the annual UN climate talks . This year, the summit will be hosted by Turkey, but in an unusual twist the negotiations will be presided over by Australia in a compromise deal struck after the two countries vied for the presidency.
